lessons.title: Why every organisation needs an AI policy
lessons.subtitle: Shadow AI, Samsung and Article 4

sections.title: The problem: shadow AI
sections.content:
> **At work:** This block is for people who implement or govern AI use in an organization. The template is a starting point and must be adapted to the jurisdiction, sector, worker representation, contracts, and existing security controls.

Shadow AI means AI services or functions used outside the approved inventory and intended controls. The risk is not limited to free chat services. Browser extensions, embedded writing features, meeting bots, and locally installed models can also create unknown data flows and unclear accountability.

A policy creates a reviewable framework: Which purposes are allowed? Which systems and features are approved? Which data, recipients, and decisions are involved? Who reviews new cases and handles incidents?

The document alone does not prevent misuse. It must connect to the inventory, technical controls, training, procurement, data protection, information security, and an accessible approval process.
sections.keyTakeaway: Shadow AI operates outside the approved inventory and intended controls. A policy works only with accountable owners, technical controls, and a usable approval process.

sections.title: The obligation: Article 4 since February 2025
sections.content:
Article 4 of the EU AI Act has applied since 2 February 2025. Following the amendment made by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, providers and deployers must take measures to support the development of AI literacy among their staff and other people dealing with the operation and use of AI systems on their behalf. Technical knowledge, experience, education and training, use context, and affected people or groups must be taken into account. Providers and deployers do not have to guarantee a specific level of competence for each individual. Nor does the law prescribe a standard certificate or fixed training format.

What does this mean in practice? Providers and deployers need traceable elements: roles, permitted tools, data rules, review procedures, escalation and learning records. An AI policy is one important part of this documentation.

This policy is not complete evidence of Article 4 compliance. It records which tools are approved, which data may be entered into which tool, how outputs are checked and what happens after an incident. Depending on the use case, the organisation may also need training, an inventory, risk classification, a data protection review and other internal procedures.
sections.keyTakeaway: Article 4 has applied since 2 February 2025. An AI policy is one documented element of AI literacy measures, not complete evidence of Article 4 compliance.

quiz.questionText: Since when has Article 4 of the EU AI Act applied?

answerOptions.text: Since 1 January 2024
Since 2 February 2025
From August 2026
It is not yet in force

quiz.explanation: Article 4 of the EU AI Act has applied since 2 February 2025. In its current form, it requires providers and deployers to take measures supporting the development of AI literacy among people acting on their behalf.

quiz.questionText: Which description of shadow AI is most accurate?

answerOptions.text: Only AI systems that run at night
Every local AI installation, including approved ones
AI services or functions used outside the approved inventory and intended controls
Only free chat services without user accounts

quiz.explanation: Shadow AI is not defined by price, provider, or hosting location. The issue is that the use, purpose, data flow, or accountability falls outside approved controls.

lessons.title: The six parts of your AI policy
lessons.subtitle: An adaptable baseline for responsibilities and rules

sections.title: Parts 1 to 3: scope, tools and data
sections.content:
This template uses six sections. It is not a universally complete compliance framework; a specific use may also require procurement, copyright, product-safety, high-risk-system, transparency, worker-representation, or export-control provisions.

**1. Scope and definitions:** Which people, entities, systems, functions, and use types does the document cover?

**2. Inventory and approvals:** Which exact product version, feature, configuration, and integration is approved for which purpose? Who owns the decision?

**3. Data and decision rules:** Which data classes, rights, recipients, and impacts are permitted? Which uses are prohibited or require case-specific review?
sections.keyTakeaway: The first three sections define scope, specific system approvals, and data and decision rules. Product names alone are insufficient.

sections.title: Parts 4 to 6: review, escalation and maintenance
sections.content:
**4. Review and human responsibility:** Which controls apply at each impact level? Who may approve the result, and when is dual control or specialist legal, security, or domain review required?

**5. Incidents and escalation:** Which internal reporting channel applies? Which information and evidence must be preserved? Who assesses a data breach, security incident, faulty decision, or provider event?

**6. Ownership, changes, and review:** Who maintains the policy and inventory? Which events trigger immediate review? How are versions, approvals, and communication documented?

The necessary detail depends on the organization and risk. A short policy can work when the inventory, approval matrix, and operating procedures are maintained separately and linked unambiguously.
sections.keyTakeaway: Parts 4 to 6 cover quality control, incident management and continuing maintenance. All six parts build on the previous blocks.

quiz.questionText: How many baseline sections does this course template use?

answerOptions.text: 3 parts
4 parts
6 parts
10 parts

quiz.explanation: The course template uses six baseline sections. It is an adaptable structure, not a guarantee of legal or organizational completeness.

quiz.questionText: Which part of the AI policy is based directly on the three-step review from block 4?

answerOptions.text: Part 2: Approved tools
Part 3: Data rules
Part 4: Review requirement
Part 6: Review cycle

quiz.explanation: Part 4 adopts the three baseline questions from block 4: factual accuracy, completeness, and suitability. The policy then assigns review depth, approval roles, and additional controls by purpose and impact.

lessons.title: Exercise: complete the policy
lessons.subtitle: Create your AI usage policy step by step

sections.title: The template: scope, tools and data
sections.content:
Complete the template with the responsible functions. Replace every bracketed placeholder before approval.

**1. Scope:** [Organization] specifies which workers, contractors, sites, systems, functions, and work devices the policy covers. Link the definitions to the current AI inventory.

**2. Approval matrix:** For each entry, record the product, version or tier, feature, integration, purpose, data classes, responsible person, contract, region, retention, permissions, and approval date. Combinations of purpose, feature, and data class that are not listed remain blocked pending review. Price and brand are not control criteria.

**3. Data and decision rules:** Refer to the organization's classification policy. Add data minimization, rights in content, permitted recipients, prohibited secrets and credentials, and rules for decisions affecting people. Define an accessible route for uncertainty.
sections.keyTakeaway: The approval matrix links purpose, feature, data class, contract, configuration, and accountability. Neither free nor enterprise is a security category by itself.

sections.title: Review requirement, escalation and signatures
sections.content:
**4. Review and approval:** Define controls by impact: source checks, calculation verification, specialist approval, dual control, or a prohibition on automated decisions. Name the person accountable for the final result.

**5. Incident reporting:** Workers report suspected misuse without delay through [reporting channel] and preserve the time, system, account, input data, output, and actions already taken. They do not delete or alter evidence on their own. [Incident Response], information security, data protection, and other responsible functions assess the case under the existing procedure.

For a personal data breach, the controller assesses whether the risk triggers notification under GDPR Article 33. Where notification is required, it is made without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours after the controller became aware. Internal deadlines belong in the incident-response plan; this template does not invent four- or 24-hour stages.

**6. Ownership and review:** Name [Policy Owner], the regular review date, and events that trigger immediate review, including new features, changed contracts, incidents, or legal changes. Record the version, approvers, effective date, and communication. Required approvals follow the organization's governance; fixed signature roles are not universal.
sections.keyTakeaway: The policy names risk-based controls, an immediately usable reporting channel, responsible decision-makers, and documented review triggers.

quiz.questionText: Why does the policy prohibit free AI tools such as ChatGPT Free?

answerOptions.text: Because they produce worse results than paid versions
Because unapproved consumer products generally offer no DPA reviewed by the organisation and no binding configuration for data use
Because they are available only in English
Because they require an internet connection

quiz.explanation: With unapproved consumer products, the organisation generally lacks a reviewed DPA, binding data controls and an agreed data region. Whether inputs may be used for training depends on the particular product and its settings.

quiz.questionText: Which statement accurately describes GDPR Article 33?

answerOptions.text: Every processing error must be reported externally within 24 hours
Only the employee involved decides whether notification is required
The controller assesses the risk; if notification is required, it is made without undue delay and where feasible within 72 hours after awareness
Notification is allowed only after the technical investigation is complete

quiz.explanation: Article 33 links notification to a personal data breach and the risk assessment. The 72-hour period starts when the controller becomes aware and is not a universal internal escalation schedule.

lessons.title: Summary
lessons.subtitle: Your five documents at a glance

sections.title: Five documents, one system
sections.content:
The course provides five working artifacts:

1. **AI inventory** with concrete functions, purposes, data, and owners.
2. **Example data classification** that must be adapted to the organization.
3. **Four task patterns** for email, meetings, data analysis, and reports.
4. **Output review** as a baseline for risk-based controls.
5. **AI usage policy** as the linking governance document.

An artifact is ready for use only after placeholders have been replaced, assumptions reviewed, owners named, and required approvals documented.
sections.keyTakeaway: The five artifacts are working materials. Organization-specific review, ownership, and documented approval make them operational.

sections.title: Next steps
sections.content:
This policy can be one documented element of AI literacy measures under Article 4. Before it takes effect:

1. **Review and approve:** Include the functions responsible under governance, data protection, information security, procurement, and worker representation.
2. **Connect operations:** Link the inventory, approval matrix, technical controls, procurement, and incident response unambiguously.
3. **Teach by role:** Affected people must be able to apply permitted purposes, boundaries, review duties, and the reporting channel.
4. **Control review:** Document a risk-based regular date and immediate review triggers.

Effectiveness is not shown by a signature. It is shown when people can find the correct approval, systems enforce boundaries, and incidents are reported and handled.
sections.keyTakeaway: Effectiveness comes from approved ownership, technical implementation, role-based application, and documented reviews.

quiz.questionText: How many documents do you create over the full AI Fundamentals course?

answerOptions.text: 2 documents
3 documents
5 documents
8 documents

quiz.explanation: The five blocks produce five documents: the AI inventory, data-classification card, prompt templates, three-step review and AI usage policy.

quiz.questionText: What is the most important next step after creating the AI policy?

answerOptions.text: File the policy and retrieve it only when needed
Have the responsible functions review it, connect it to operations, teach it by role, and define review triggers
Wait until the EU issues further requirements
Hire an external consultant to implement it

quiz.explanation: A policy works only when responsible functions approve it, operational controls implement it, affected people can apply it, and defined events trigger review.
